facts.text: On Nov 17, 1869, the Suez Canal opened — cutting the London-to-Mumbai sea route by 7,000 km and reshaping global trade within a decade.
On Nov 17, 1800, the U.S. Congress met in Washington D.C. for the first time. The city had been a swamp-filled construction site just months before.
Indonesia spans more time zones than the continental United States — its 17,000 islands stretch across three, covering a horizontal distance wider than the lower 48 states.
Manila is the most densely populated city on Earth, packing over 111,000 people per square kilometer — denser than any neighborhood in New York or Tokyo.
More people live inside a circle drawn 4,000 km around Bangkok than outside it — over half of humanity fits within that single ring.

On this date in 1869, the Suez Canal opened for navigation — instantly slashing the London-to-Bombay shipping route by 4,500 miles and making British imperial trade economics work in ways they simply hadn't before.
On this date in 1993, the U.S. House passed NAFTA by just 34 votes. The deal eventually grew into a $1.3 trillion annual trade relationship between three countries.

The NYSE's famously chaotic open-outcry trading floor employed roughly 5,000 people in 2000. By 2020, fewer than 500 remained — replaced not by silence, but by algorithms completing millions of trades per second.
Berkshire Hathaway's original business was a failing textile mill. Warren Buffett later called buying it the worst investment of his life — a $200 billion lesson in sunk-cost thinking.
Saudi Aramco's 2019 IPO raised $25.6 billion, the largest in history. It also valued the company at $1.7 trillion, briefly making it worth more than the entire German stock market.
On this date in 1970, the Soviet Lunokhod 1 became the first remote-controlled rover to operate on another world — it outlasted its planned 3-month mission by nearly a year.
On this date in 1869, the Suez Canal opened, but the physics mattered: it has no locks because the Red Sea and Mediterranean sit at nearly identical sea levels.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city — a single teaspoon of its material would weigh about a billion tons on Earth.
Your body contains roughly 37 trillion cells, yet the electrical signal commanding your hand to move travels from brain to fingertip in under 20 milliseconds.
Mantis shrimp see with 16 types of photoreceptors compared to the human eye's 3 — yet research shows they process color worse than humans, not better.
On this day in 1869, the Suez Canal opened — connecting seas that humans had tried to link since the Pharaohs. The project killed an estimated 120,000 workers.
Oxford University was teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. Oxford dates to 1096; Tenochtitlán wasn't founded until 1325.
On this day in 1558, Elizabeth I became Queen of England. She would outlast four assassination plots, two serious suitors, and everyone who underestimated her.
The fax machine was invented in 1843 — 33 years before the telephone. Alexander Bain patented it while most of the world was still moving information by horse.
Nintendo was founded in 1889, when Grover Cleveland was U.S. president and the Eiffel Tower was brand new. It spent its first 85 years selling playing cards.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in 2012, it spread so fast it feels ancient.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh word for a homesickness for a home you cannot return to — or never had. No single English word comes close.
Vellichor (n.): the strange wistfulness of used bookshops. Another Koenig coinage, proof that naming a feeling is halfway to owning it.
On this day in 1869, the Suez Canal opened — and the word 'isthmian' briefly surged in print, meaning 'of or relating to an isthmus,' from Greek isthmos, a narrow neck of land.
On this day in 1558, Mary I of England died, and Elizabeth I was proclaimed queen. The era that followed gave English 'gloriana' — a radiant, almost divine feminine power — from the Latin gloria.
On this day in 2021, Ethereum's EIP-1559 had burned over 1 million ETH in its first 100 days — permanently removing from supply the equivalent of roughly three years of pre-merge miner rewards.
On this day in 2013, Bitcoin crossed $1,000 on Mt. Gox for the first time, a price level it would not sustainably reclaim for nearly four years.
Bitcoin's timelock primitive, nLockTime, was present in the very first version of the protocol — Satoshi included a mechanism for future-dated transactions before anyone had a use case for it.
The largest single Bitcoin transaction by value was 500,000 BTC moved in 2011 for a fee of 0.1 BTC — the sender was almost certainly consolidating exchange cold storage, not settling a trade.
Ethereum's state trie stores every contract and account balance as a node in a Merkle Patricia tree, meaning a single changed byte anywhere in global state produces a completely different root hash.

On this date in 2022, OpenAI launched ChatGPT. It reached 1 million users in 5 days — faster than any consumer product in history — and rewrote the deployment assumptions of nearly every AI lab within weeks.

On this date in 2023, Sam Altman was fired as OpenAI CEO, then reinstated five days later after roughly 700 of 770 employees threatened to quit. The board cited loss of confidence; the actual deliberations remain undisclosed.
AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins — essentially the entire known proteome — in 2022. Structural biologists had spent decades solving roughly 170,000 by hand.

The original GPT-3 training run consumed an estimated 1,287 MWh of electricity. A single H100 GPU cluster training a frontier model today can draw more power than a small city district, continuously, for months.

Backpropagation was described in a 1986 Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams paper in Nature. The core algorithm had existed in various forms since the 1960s — the field simply lacked the data and hardware to make it matter.
